paragraphs.title: The Threat to Jabesh-gilead and the Request for Time

easy.explanation: The passage says that Nahash the Ammonite encamped against Jabesh-gilead.
easy.q: Who came up and encamped against Jabesh-gilead?

easy.explanation: The men of Jabesh asked Nahash to make a covenant with them.
easy.q: What did the men of Jabesh ask Nahash to make with them?

easy.explanation: The elders asked for seven days to send messengers throughout Israel.
easy.q: How many days of respite did the elders of Jabesh request?

medium.explanation: They said, “Make a covenant with us, and we will serve thee.”
medium.q: What did the men of Jabesh agree to do if Nahash made the covenant?

medium.explanation: Nahash said that he would thrust out all their right eyes.
medium.q: What did Nahash threaten to do to the right eyes of the men of Jabesh?

answers: To send messengers throughout Israel for help
medium.explanation: They wanted time to send messengers to all the coasts of Israel.
medium.q: Why did the elders ask for seven days?

answers: They were seeking a way to avoid immediate battle
They wanted to join the Ammonites permanently
challenge.explanation: Their request suggests that they were trying to avoid immediate destruction and gain time.
challenge.q: What does the request for a covenant show about the men of Jabesh at that moment?

answers: The elders asked for time, then Nahash came, then the city was besieged
Nahash encamped, offered a humiliating condition, and the elders requested seven days
The men of Jabesh attacked Nahash, then asked for a covenant
challenge.explanation: Nahash first encamped against the city, then gave his condition, and the elders asked for time.
challenge.q: Which sequence correctly describes the events in these verses?

answers: The crisis was viewed as a concern for all Israel
Only Jabesh was responsible for the problem
challenge.explanation: The elders appealed to the whole nation, showing that the threat was regarded as a national concern.
challenge.q: What does sending messengers to all the coasts of Israel indicate?

paragraphs.title: Saul Rises to Leadership and Mobilizes the People

easy.explanation: The people lifted up their voices and wept.
easy.q: How did the people at Gibeah respond when they heard the news?

easy.explanation: Saul came after the herd out of the field.
easy.q: Where had Saul come from when he asked why the people were weeping?

easy.explanation: The children of Israel numbered three hundred thousand.
easy.q: How many children of Israel were numbered at Bezek?

answers: Hearing the news about the men of Jabesh
medium.explanation: The Spirit of God came upon Saul when he heard the news, and his anger was greatly kindled.
medium.q: What caused Saul’s anger to become greatly kindled?

answers: By sending pieces of oxen throughout the land
By calling only the people at Gilgal
medium.explanation: Saul hewed a yoke of oxen in pieces and sent them throughout Israel as a summons.
medium.q: How did Saul summon the people throughout Israel?

answers: They came out with one consent
medium.explanation: The people came out with one consent.
medium.q: What was the result of the fear of the Lord falling upon the people?

answers: He changes from a man returning from the field into a national leader
He becomes a servant of Nahash
challenge.explanation: Saul moves from ordinary work in the field to leading and mobilizing Israel.
challenge.q: What major change occurs in Saul’s role in these verses?

answers: They warned that those who refused to follow would face a similar judgment
They provided food for the army
They marked the location of the camp
challenge.explanation: The message warned that the oxen of anyone who did not come after Saul and Samuel would be treated likewise.
challenge.q: Why were the pieces of the oxen an effective summons?

answers: Israel had thirty thousand and Judah three hundred thousand
Israel had three hundred thousand and Judah thirty thousand
Both groups had the same number
challenge.explanation: Three hundred thousand were numbered from Israel, and thirty thousand from Judah.
challenge.q: What distinction is given between the numbers from Israel and Judah?

paragraphs.title: The Deception and the Attack on the Ammonite Camp

easy.explanation: The messengers told them, “To morrow... ye shall have help.”
easy.q: What message was sent to the men of Jabesh?

easy.explanation: The army came into the midst of the host in the morning watch.
easy.q: When did Saul’s army enter the Ammonite camp?

easy.explanation: Saul put the people in three companies.
easy.q: Into how many companies did Saul divide the people?

answers: They told the Ammonites they would come out the next day
They asked Nahash for another seven days
medium.explanation: They said they would come out on the next day, giving Saul’s army time to prepare.
medium.q: How did the men of Jabesh gain time?

medium.explanation: The messengers showed them the news, and they were glad.
medium.q: How did the men of Jabesh respond when they heard about the coming help?

answers: They were scattered so that two of them were not left together
They made a covenant with Israel
medium.explanation: The Ammonites were scattered until two of them were not left together.
medium.q: What happened to the Ammonites after Saul’s attack?

answers: It helped them surprise and overwhelm the Ammonites
It allowed the Ammonites to prepare
It prevented Saul’s army from reaching the camp
challenge.explanation: The early attack, following the deception, enabled Saul’s army to strike by surprise.
challenge.q: What advantage did the morning attack give Saul’s army?

answers: It allowed an organized attack from several directions
It identified three kings among the Ammonites
It provided three days of rest
challenge.explanation: The three companies formed part of Saul’s organized battle strategy.
challenge.q: How did dividing the army into three companies contribute to the battle?

answers: They received hope when they learned that help was coming
They forgot the threat against them
challenge.explanation: Their gladness came after they learned that Saul’s army would deliver them.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the movement of the men of Jabesh from sorrow to gladness?

easy.explanation: The people asked Samuel to bring the men so that they might put them to death.
easy.q: What did the people want to do to the men who had questioned Saul’s reign?

easy.explanation: Saul said that no man should be put to death that day.
easy.q: Who prevented the execution of Saul’s opponents?

easy.explanation: Saul declared, “to day the Lord hath wrought salvation in Israel.”
easy.q: What did Saul say the Lord had wrought in Israel?

answers: The day was a day of the Lord’s salvation and should not become a day of vengeance
The people had refused to fight
medium.explanation: Saul focused attention on the Lord’s salvation rather than on punishing his former opponents.
medium.q: Why did Saul refuse to take revenge on his opponents?

answers: He joined the men who opposed him
medium.explanation: Saul used his authority to stop the people from carrying out revenge.
medium.q: What does Saul’s statement that no man should be put to death reveal about his leadership?

medium.explanation: Saul explicitly said that the Lord had wrought salvation in Israel.
medium.q: To whom did Saul attribute the victory?

answers: The people wanted revenge, while Saul prevented it
The people wanted peace, while Saul wanted surrender
The people wanted to flee, while Saul wanted to serve Nahash
challenge.explanation: The people wanted the opponents executed, but Saul stopped the revenge.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast between the people’s response and Saul’s response?

answers: It prevented division after the victory
It separated the people into rival groups
challenge.explanation: Mercy toward the opponents allowed the nation to remain united after the battle.
challenge.q: How could Saul’s decision strengthen unity in Israel?

answers: He credited divine help rather than only his own military leadership
He announced that the battle had not begun
He denied that the army had any role
challenge.explanation: Saul presented the victory as the Lord’s salvation in Israel.
challenge.q: Why is it significant that Saul mentioned the Lord after the victory?

easy.explanation: Samuel told the people to go to Gilgal.
easy.q: Where did Samuel tell the people to go?

easy.explanation: Samuel said, “let us go to Gilgal, and renew the kingdom there.”
easy.q: What did Samuel say they should renew there?

easy.explanation: They sacrificed sacrifices of peace offerings before the Lord.
easy.q: What did the people sacrifice before the Lord?

medium.explanation: Samuel instructed the people to go to Gilgal.
medium.q: Who led the people to Gilgal?

answers: They made Saul king and offered peace offerings
They divided the army into three companies
medium.explanation: They made Saul king before the Lord and sacrificed peace offerings.
medium.q: What did the people do at Gilgal?

medium.explanation: The passage says that Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.
medium.q: How did Saul and the men of Israel feel at Gilgal?

answers: The victory provided an opportunity to confirm Saul’s leadership
The victory showed that a king was no longer needed
The victory transferred the kingdom to Nahash
challenge.explanation: Saul’s leadership had been demonstrated in action, so the people renewed his kingship.
challenge.q: Why was the kingdom renewed after the victory over Ammon?

answers: It presents the event as having religious significance
It places the event inside the Ammonite camp
It shows that Saul was absent
challenge.explanation: The phrase connects Saul’s kingship with worship and recognition before the Lord.
challenge.q: What does the phrase “before the Lord” add to the account of Saul’s kingship?

answers: The people went to Gilgal, renewed the kingdom, offered sacrifices, and rejoiced
The people wept, endured a siege, requested seven days, and fled
The people surrendered, made a covenant with Ammon, and scattered
challenge.explanation: The chapter ends with the assembly at Gilgal, the renewal of Saul’s kingship, offerings, and great rejoicing.
challenge.q: Which sequence best summarizes the end of the chapter?
